props.title: Background to Danger

sections.content: Background to Danger emerges from Warner Bros.' wave of WWII-era spy thrillers, following the success of Casablanca (1942). Director Raoul Walsh, known for his dynamic action sequences in films like High Sierra (1941), brings his signature intensity to this adaptation of Eric Ambler's novel. The film stars George Raft as an American agent in Turkey who becomes entangled in Nazi espionage, with Sydney Greenstreet and Peter Lorre providing crucial supporting performances that echo their earlier pairing in The Maltese Falcon (1941).

sections.content: The film exemplifies Hollywood's wartime pivot to anti-Nazi propaganda pieces, joining contemporaries like Confessions of a Nazi Spy (1939) and All Through the Night (1942). Walsh's direction emphasizes action over the novel's more cerebral approach, creating a fast-paced thriller that prioritizes entertainment over political complexity. The Turkish setting provides an exotic backdrop while highlighting the strategic importance of neutral nations during WWII, a theme also explored in Five Graves to Cairo (1943).

Sydney Greenstreet and Peter Lorre's presence connects Background to Danger to a broader cycle of Warner Bros. espionage films. Their chemistry, first showcased in The Maltese Falcon (1941), became a reliable draw for audiences, leading to further collaborations like The Conspirators (1944) and Three Strangers (1946). George Raft's casting represents Warner's attempt to create a more action-oriented spy hero, contrasting with the more sophisticated personas of actors like William Powell. movies.slug: Bette Davis stars in this wartime thriller about Nazi agents in America

sections.content: The film's production coincided with Hollywood's broader effort to support the war effort through entertainment. Unlike the more overt propaganda of films like Mission to Moscow (1943), Background to Danger wraps its message in the familiar tropes of the spy thriller. The film's treatment of Nazi agents as straightforward villains reflects the industry's shift away from the moral ambiguity found in pre-war espionage films like The Lady Vanishes (1938).
